entry.title: Rahimi and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2400
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Rahimi’s Class XB Subclass 201 visa under s 501CA(4). Mr Rahimi failed the character test due to a 15-month aggregate sentence, but the Tribunal set aside the delegate’s decision and revoked the cancellation. The case turned on the Direction No 110 balancing, especially mental health, family support and risk of reoffending.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: CMTWN and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2399
entry.content:
In CMTWN and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2399, the applicant sought review of an NDIA decision dated 27 May 2026 concerning NDIS plan variations. The Tribunal found the application did not seek review of an internal review decision under s 100(6) of the NDIS Act when filed and was premature. It dismissed the application under s 97 of the ART Act and held it had no power to treat the submissions as a new application.

Key holding: Where an application does not seek review of a reviewable decision, the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction and must dismiss it under s 97 of the ART Act.

The Tribunal must dismiss an application if: (a) the application is made for review of a decision; and (b) the Tribunal is satisfied that the decision is not reviewable by the Tribunal.

entry.title: Xi and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2397
entry.content:
The applicant, a Chinese national, had his Resident Return (Class BB) (Subclass 155) visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) after being sentenced to 48 months’ imprisonment for offences arising from a cybercrime scam syndicate and firearm possession. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation under s 501CA(4), and the Tribunal affirmed that decision. The Tribunal found the offending serious and that community protection and expectations outweighed a low risk of reoffending and the applicant’s ties.

Key holding: Serious offending may cause the community expectations consideration under Direction No 110 to weigh significantly against revocation despite an applicant’s personal circumstances.

In the present case, the Tribunal has found the applicant's offending is serious. Taking into consideration the personal circumstances of the applicant, it considers this consideration weighs significantly against revocation of the cancellation.

entry.title: Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2396
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.

Key holding: A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. I consider that the 'residual' risk of reoffending is acceptable despite the potentially serious consequences for the community, and Mr Hoang's length of residence from a young age must take into account.

entry.title: FWKPM and Chief Executive Officer, National Insurance Disability Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2402
entry.content:
In FWKPM and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2402, an NDIS review required determination of whether three summonses should issue to two schools and a support-coordination provider. A Registrar refused the requests on excessive-scope and privacy grounds, but the Tribunal held the documents were apparently relevant and privacy did not justify refusal. The Tribunal issued all three summonses with a return date of 30 October 2026.

Key holding: Where documents are of apparent relevance and no party objects, the Tribunal should ordinarily exercise its discretion to issue a summons unless the summons is vexatious, frivolous or otherwise an abuse of process.

I would add one further observation, namely that generally speaking where a party asks for a summons, the documents sought are of apparent relevance, and no other party objects to the summons being issued, the discretion to issue a summons should ordinarily be exercised, unless it vexatious or frivolous or otherwise an abuse of process to issue the summons.

entry.title: XTXD and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2401
entry.content:
The Administrative Review Tribunal dealt with two second-review applications concerning the percentage of care for a child in a child support assessment. The Father alleged care changed in March 2024 and again in September 2024, while the Mother disputed his account. The Tribunal found an approximate 50/50 care pattern from 7 March 2024 but was not satisfied the later change to full-time care was established.

Key holding: A care percentage may be determined from an overall pattern of recurring care despite an irregular timetable, without identifying every overnight occasion.

An irregular arrangement can constitute a pattern of care where the evidence establishes recurring care, even though the precise timetable of care changes.

entry.title: WNZP and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2398
entry.content:
This was a second review in a child support matter concerning the parents’ percentage of care for two children after the Mother notified a change of care on 23 March 2024. The Tribunal recalculated actual care, rejected an argument that the Father’s overseas absences meant he had relinquished care, and declined to record court-ordered care under s 51 because the change predated 29 March 2024. The decision under review was set aside and new care percentages were substituted.

Key holding: Under the law applying before 29 March 2024, an interim care determination under s 51 cannot be made where existing care percentages are revoked under s 54F or s 54H.

I am bound by the Court's interpretation in CMU23 and must apply the legislation in force prior to 29 March 2024, specifically paragraph 53(1)(c), such that an interim determination cannot be made when existing percentages of care are revoked either pursuant to section 54F or section 54H of the Act.

entry.title: Latif and Commissioner of the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2342
entry.content:
The Tribunal refused the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission’s application to dismiss Mr Latif’s review applications concerning deemed internal review decisions to affirm a permanent ban and registration renewal refusal for Horizon Solsolutions Australia Pty Ltd. The case concerned whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction, whether Mr Latif was “directly affected”, and whether deemed decisions arose under the ART Act. The dismissal application was dismissed, so the substantive review applications remain on foot.

Key holding: A decision-maker cannot isolate a separate non-reviewable “standing” decision from the NDIS Act s 100 internal review process; standing is a threshold matter within that process and may be assessed by the Tribunal in determining jurisdiction.

It is my characterisation that the issue of standing is inherently a threshold matter that should be addressed as an integral part of the internal review process under s 100 of the NDIS Act, rather than as a distinct and, in this case as submitted by the Respondent, a non-reviewable decision made under s 100(2) of that Act.

entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: CYZGC by his plan nominee and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2332
entry.content:
The applicant, a 10-year-old NDIS participant, sought interim relief after a reassessment increased his core supports but reduced his therapy funding and added behaviour support. He asked the Tribunal under s 32(2) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth) to reallocate or make flexible the behaviour support funding, or alternatively to stay Plan-2 so Plan-1 revived. The Tribunal refused, finding neither order desirable to ensure the effectiveness of the review, and recommended an early conference and hearing.

Key holding: Under s 32(2) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), an interim stay or other order is made only if desirable to ensure the effectiveness of the review; hardship, even serious hardship, is insufficient unless it puts the effectiveness of the review in jeopardy.

Finally, in relation to hardship, it is not enough that the decision causes hardship, even serious hardship. The discretion may only be exercised where the degree of hardship is such that it puts the effectiveness of the review in jeopardy.[5]

entry.title: LFQR and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security second review) [2026] ARTA 2320
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal to pay family tax benefit top ups and supplements for 2022/23 because the applicant’s partner lodged his income tax return on 4 July 2024, after the 30 June 2024 reconciliation deadline. The applicant relied on stress, family violence, alcohol issues, a brief separation and pandemic-related pressures. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no special circumstances that prevented the partner from lodging on time.

Key holding: Under s 32D(1)(c)(ii) of the Administration Act, special circumstances will only extend the reconciliation time if they actually prevented the partner from lodging the income tax return by the required date.

For the Applicant to be paid top ups and supplements of family tax benefit for 2022/23, the Tribunal must be satisfied that there are special circumstances that prevented the Applicant's partner from lodging his income tax return by 30 June 2024.

entry.title: Jaworski v Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 213
entry.content:
Mr Jaworski sought to set aside or vary the Court of Appeal’s earlier leave judgment under UCPR r 36.16, and CA ANZ sought gross sum costs. The Court dismissed the reopening application and fixed costs at $30,000 for the leave/recusal application and $6,000 for CA ANZ’s notice of motion. The dispute concerned alleged errors, bias/prejudgment and costs in ongoing litigation involving CA ANZ.

Key holding: Under UCPR r 36.16, reopening requires some error in the court's reasoning due to misapprehension of fact or law that is not solely attributable to the applicant's neglect or default.

What is required to be established on an application under r 36.16 is some error in the court's reasoning because of a misapprehension of the facts or misapprehension of the relevant law; and that this misapprehension cannot be attributed solely to the neglect or default of the party seeking the rehearing.

entry.title: South Australian Commission for Catholic Schools Inc and Secretary, Department of Education (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2304
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed 2024 Commonwealth recurrent funding determinations for 84 non-government Catholic schools in South Australia. It unanimously held that mid-year reception students who began in term 3 2024 were “primary students” because reception was the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1. A majority then held those students did not have a pattern of regular attendance at school or school generally during 2024, so they failed reg 9B(1)(c) and were ineligible unless the Minister included them under reg 9B(3).

Key holding: Reception undertaken by mid-year reception students is the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1, so those students are primary students in that calendar year.

Giving the phrases to which I have already referred their natural meaning, the logical conclusion is that the 2024 mid-year reception students were in the year of schooling in a course of primary education that was immediately before year 1. It follows that, in 2024, those students were in the foundation year of schooling, were receiving primary education and were therefore primary students at their school.

The Tribunal is satisfied that the discretion under subsection 56(1) of the NVR Act not to cancel the Qualification can be safely and appropriately exercised in the exceptional circumstances of this case. entry.title: VBCW and Commissioner of Taxation (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2312
entry.content:
This was an interlocutory tax review proceeding in the Administrative Review Tribunal. The Applicant sought to amend his Statement of Facts, Issues and Contentions and to expand his grounds of objection concerning trust distributions, Division 40 deductions, balancing adjustment events, and management fees allegedly deductible under s 8-1 of the ITAA 1997. entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a Centrelink decision raising a $4,109.18 newstart allowance debt against Mr Kirby for 30 November 2018 to 1 April 2019 due to undeclared employment income. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the matter because Centrelink’s earlier income apportionment was not the method required under s 1117D(9) of the Social Security Act 1991. Any recalculated overpayment remains a Commonwealth debt and recovery was not waived.

Key holding: Where pre-7 December 2020 Division 3 work income is reviewed and neither the entitlement period in which it was earned nor the payroll period can be identified, it must be assessed under s 1117D(9) in the entitlement period in which it was received.

This means that the third approach in subsection 1117D(9) must be used so that [Mr Kirby's] wages are to be assessed on each day of the newstart allowance entitlement period in which he received the income.

entry.title: 2532892 (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2389
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal of a Child (Migrant) (Class AH) Subclass 101 visa for an applicant over 18 who was not in a relationship or full-time work and who completed high school in June 2023 but did not start full-time study until December 2023, after the visa application was lodged on 4 August 2023. The Tribunal accepted the study gap was exceptional and beyond his control but held it had no discretion because binding authority requires actual commencement of full-time study by the time of application. It affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: Under cl 101.213(1)(c), a Subclass 101 applicant over 18 must have actually commenced the relevant full-time course of study by the time the visa application is lodged, and the six-month/reasonable-time grace period does not remove that requirement.

The Court held that cl 101.213(1)(c) requires that a visa applicant must have actually commenced a full-time course of study by the time the visa application is lodged and to construe the statutory provision otherwise was to re-write the words 'been undertaking'.

entry.title: Harvey and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2293
entry.content:
In Harvey and Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] ARTA 2293, Mrs Harvey sought review of a Centrelink decision raising and recovering an FTB debt of $4,106.55 for 2023–24 after her actual adjusted taxable income exceeded her estimates. The Tribunal found the overpayment was correctly calculated under s 71 and that neither administrative-error waiver nor discretionary waiver applied. It affirmed the decision under review.

Key holding: For discretionary waiver under s 101, special circumstances require the individual circumstances to be outside the usual or ordinary course; mere inadvertence, financial hardship or administrative delay will not suffice.

Special circumstances' is not a term defined in the legislation. For waiver on the basis of special circumstances to apply, it is necessary to examine the individual circumstances of the case and find something about a person's circumstances to take their situation out of the usual or ordinary course (for example, Dranichnikov v Centrelink [2003] FCAFC 133).

entry.title: Rushpinder Kaur (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2367
entry.content:
This is a review of a delegate's refusal of a Subclass 500 (Student) visa on the basis that the applicant, a 23-year-old Indian national, was not a genuine temporary entrant. The Tribunal accepted the applicant's evidence as frank and credible, found her family ties in India and the value of her Australian study outweighed her stronger Australian earnings, and remitted the matter. It is a fact-focused GTE decision with no new legal principle.

Key holding: In assessing the genuine temporary entrant criterion, the Direction No. 108 factors are guides only rather than a checklist, and the decision maker must determine on balance whether the applicant satisfies the criterion having regard to all the circumstances.

The Direction indicates that the factors specified should not be used as a checklist but rather, are intended only to guide decision makers when considering the applicant's circumstances as a whole, in reaching a finding about whether the applicant satisfies the genuine temporary entrant criterion.

entry.title: Lind and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2296
entry.content:
In Lind and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2296, Ms Lind sought review of Centrelink’s suspension of her jobseeker payment while she travelled to [Country 1] to visit her mother after a hip fracture. The Tribunal considered whether her absence was for an approved portability reason, specifically an acute family crisis. The Tribunal affirmed the suspension because her mother was not critically ill or hospitalised at the time Ms Lind departed Australia.

Key holding: Jobseeker payment is portable for an acute family crisis only where the absence is for visiting a family member who is critically ill, meaning their condition is severe or grave or there is a crisis in the condition.

Although the Act does not define what constitutes being critically ill, the case law indicates that "critically" must be given its ordinary meaning and that a person's condition must be severe or grave or that there must be a crisis in the condition - see, for example, Al Umari and Secretary, DFaCS [2003] AATA 431.

entry.title: Fearon and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2294
entry.content:
Ms Fearon receives age pension. Centrelink treated $70,500 she effectively gifted to her daughter in December 2022 as a deprived asset. The Tribunal affirmed that decision, finding the gifting rules required the amount to be included in her assets for five years.

Key holding: A disposal of an asset, including money, for no or inadequate consideration must be included as an asset for five years from the date of disposition.

The legislation is clear, where an asset (which includes money) has been disposed of for no or inadequate consideration, it must be included as an asset for five years from the date of disposition.

entry.title: Scrubb and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security) [2026] ARTA 2290
entry.content:
Mrs Scrubb sought review of a Centrelink decision declining additional child care subsidy (ACCS) for her son, [Child A], for 16 June 2025 to 14 September 2025. The Tribunal considered whether [Child A] met the “at risk of serious abuse or neglect” criterion, limited to a claimed risk of neglect. It found the risk was not real and apparent and affirmed the decision.

Key holding: For ACCS child wellbeing, a child is at risk of serious abuse or neglect only if the risk is real and apparent, not merely a hypothetical or far-fetched possibility.

Nonetheless, I accept the sense in the Guide that what 'risk' requires, in context, is a real and apparent risk. The test cannot be made out by pointing to some far-fetched possibility.

entry.title: Chambwela (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2388
entry.content:
Mr Chambwela sought review of a refusal of a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) subclass 500 visa. He had completed his Advanced Diploma of Civil Construction and Design and was awaiting graduation, but did not provide proof of current enrolment in a registered course as at the time of decision. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: A subclass 500 applicant must be enrolled in a registered course at the time of decision; having completed the course and awaiting graduation does not satisfy the enrolment requirement.

Awaiting formal graduation is not a basis for a student visa under the Act.

entry.title: Singh (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2376
entry.content:
The Tribunal reconsidered, on remittal, a delegate’s refusal of a Subclass 500 (Student) visa on genuine temporary entrant grounds under cl 500.212. Despite serious concerns about the applicant’s credibility, study gap and a PRISMS enrolment discrepancy, it accepted that he was nearing completion of his automotive studies and intended to return to India after finishing in August 2026. The Tribunal set aside the refusal and remitted the visa application for reconsideration, finding cl 500.212 met.

entry.title: JLNR and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2339
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of JLNR’s Class BB Subclass 155 resident return visa after he was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment for child exploitation material offences. JLNR conceded he did not pass the character test, so the issue was whether another reason to revoke existed under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, so the visa remains cancelled.
